title: What is a subquery, and can it return multiple rows (single-row vs multi-row vs correlated, IN/ANY/ALL)?

s1_definition.profdef: A subquery is a query nested inside another query, used to supply a value, a set of values, or a derived table to the outer query. A single-row subquery returns one value and is compared with `=`, `<`, `>`. A multi-row subquery returns many values and is used with `IN`, `ANY`, or `ALL`. A correlated subquery references a column from the outer query and is re-evaluated for each outer row.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh asks a clerk at National Bank of India: "Show me accounts with a balance above the average." The clerk first works out the average balance (an inner question), then uses that single number to filter accounts (the outer question). That inner question is a subquery. If the inner question returns one number it is single-row; if it returns a list of account ids it is multi-row and you ask "is this account IN that list?"; and if the inner question depends on each outer account one at a time, it is correlated.
s1_definition.oneliner: A subquery is a query inside a query — single-row returns one value for `=`, multi-row returns a set for `IN`/`ANY`/`ALL`, and correlated re-runs per outer row.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A subquery is a query nested inside another query, used to supply a value, a set of values, or a derived table to the outer query. A single-row subquery returns one value and is compared with `=`, `<`, `>`. A multi-row subquery returns many values and is used with `IN`, `ANY`, or `ALL`. A correlated subquery references a column from the outer query and is re-evaluated for each outer row.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh asks a clerk at National Bank of India: "Show me accounts with a balance above the average." The clerk first works out the average balance (an inner question), then uses that single number to filter accounts (the outer question). That inner question is a subquery. If the inner question returns one number it is single-row; if it returns a list of account ids it is multi-row and you ask "is this account IN that list?"; and if the inner question depends on each outer account one at a time, it is correlated.

**One line to remember:** A subquery is a query inside a query — single-row returns one value for `=`, multi-row returns a set for `IN`/`ANY`/`ALL`, and correlated re-runs per outer row.

sections.s2_technical:
A subquery can appear in several places: in the `WHERE` clause as a filter, in the `FROM` clause as a derived table, in the `SELECT` list as a scalar value, and in a `HAVING` clause.

A single-row (scalar) subquery must return exactly one row and one column. You compare it with a scalar operator. For example `WHERE balance > (SELECT AVG(balance) FROM accounts)`. If such a subquery accidentally returns more than one row, the database raises an error, so single-row subqueries demand that the inner query is guaranteed to produce one value, which is why they usually wrap an aggregate like `AVG` or `MAX`.

A multi-row subquery returns a set of values and must be used with a set operator. `IN` tests membership: `WHERE account_id IN (SELECT account_id FROM blocked_accounts)`. `ANY` (also spelled `SOME`) is true if the comparison holds for at least one value, so `> ANY (SELECT amount FROM txns)` means greater than the minimum. `ALL` is true if the comparison holds for every value, so `> ALL (...)` means greater than the maximum. A subtle point is that `= ANY` is equivalent to `IN`, and `<> ALL` is equivalent to `NOT IN`.

A correlated subquery references a column from the outer query, so it cannot be run once in isolation — it is conceptually re-evaluated for each outer row. For example `WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM txns t WHERE t.account_id = a.account_id)` checks, for each account `a`, whether it has any transaction. Correlated subqueries are powerful for existence checks and per-row comparisons, but because they run per outer row, the optimizer must be able to turn them into an efficient join or semi-join, and an index on the correlated column is essential. A senior nuance is that `NOT IN` with a subquery that can produce NULL silently returns no rows, so for "not matching" checks a correlated `NOT EXISTS` is safer than `NOT IN`.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India wants to flag "high-value" accounts whose balance exceeds the bank-wide average balance. Computing the average is one inner question returning a single number, then filtering accounts against it. This is a single-row subquery.

Problem 2 — The fraud team maintains a list of blocked account ids. They want all transactions belonging to any blocked account. "Is this transaction's account in the blocked set?" is a multi-row subquery with `IN`.

Problem 3 — The relationship team wants every account that has made at least one transaction, checked per account. That per-outer-row existence check is a correlated subquery with `EXISTS`.

Our mini-project builds a `SubqueryService` that computes all three in memory, mirroring the SQL exactly: a single-row average filter, a multi-row `IN` filter, and a correlated `EXISTS` check. It includes `Account` and `Txn` models, a repository, the service, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three accounts — Rajesh Rs.1,000,000, Priya Rs.250,000, Amit Rs.300,000. Priya is blocked. Transactions: TX1 by Rajesh, TX2 by Priya.

Step 1 — The single-row subquery first computes the average balance: (1,000,000 + 250,000 + 300,000) divided by 3 equals Rs.516,666.67. That one number is the inner result. The outer query then keeps accounts whose balance exceeds it. Only Rajesh at Rs.1,000,000 qualifies; Priya and Amit are below the average.

Step 2 — The multi-row `IN` subquery gets the blocked set {CUR3001}. The outer query checks each transaction's account against that set. TX1 belongs to Rajesh (not blocked) and is dropped. TX2 belongs to Priya (blocked) and is kept.

Step 3 — The correlated `EXISTS` subquery runs per account. For Rajesh it checks whether any transaction has his account id — TX1 does, so he is kept. For Priya, TX2 matches, so she is kept. For Amit, no transaction matches, so he is dropped. The result is Rajesh and Priya.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A subquery is simply a query nested inside another query, and it can appear in the WHERE clause as a filter, in the FROM clause as a derived table, or in the SELECT list as a scalar value. The right way to classify them is by what they return. A single-row or scalar subquery returns exactly one value and is compared with a scalar operator such as equals, greater than, or less than. The classic example at the National Bank of India is finding accounts whose balance exceeds the bank-wide average, where the inner query computes the single average value and the outer query filters against it. If a single-row subquery ever returns more than one row the database raises an error, which is why they typically wrap an aggregate like AVG or MAX.

A multi-row subquery returns a set of values, so it must be used with a set operator. `IN` tests membership, which is how we find all transactions whose account appears in the fraud team's blocked-accounts set. `ANY`, also called `SOME`, is true when the comparison holds for at least one value, so greater-than-ANY means greater than the minimum, while `ALL` is true when it holds for every value, so greater-than-ALL means greater than the maximum. Two useful equivalences are that equals-ANY is the same as `IN` and not-equal-ALL is the same as `NOT IN`.

A correlated subquery references a column from the outer query, so it cannot run on its own and is conceptually re-evaluated for each outer row. We use it for per-row existence checks, such as finding every account that has at least one transaction with `WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM txns t WHERE t.account_id = a.id)`. Because a correlated subquery runs per outer row, an index on the correlated column is essential, and the optimizer usually rewrites it into an efficient semi-join. One senior caution I always mention is that `NOT IN` against a subquery that can contain NULL silently returns no rows, so for not-matching checks a correlated `NOT EXISTS` is safer. The line I always state is that a subquery is a query inside a query — single-row returns one value for equals, multi-row returns a set for IN, ANY, or ALL, and correlated re-runs once per outer row.
